title: A morning breath
tomorrow: two young monks ask an old abba how to pray always. his answer?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first minute: in Mark, Jesus rose a great while before day and prayed before the crowd arrived. Today, something to put in that minute, something you carry everywhere already.

Breathing courses love the word advanced. The Buddha did something stranger. In the Anapanasati Sutta it's the end of the rainy-season retreat at Savatthi, and the hall is full of monks, elders like Sariputta among them. On the full-moon night the Buddha says he's so pleased with how they're practicing that he'll stay on another month. When the next full moon comes, with the elders now teaching newer monks, he looks over the silent assembly and teaches breathing in and breathing out. Why?
screen: `ADVANCED, SAYS EVERY COURSE.` → `A FULL MOON, A HALL OF ELDERS.` → `HE TEACHES… BREATHING?`

segments.voice: The answer is in how he teaches it. He doesn't say breathe better. He says a monk goes to the forest, the root of a tree or an empty hut, sits with the body straight, and then: breathing in long, he knows he breathes in long. Breathing out short, he knows he breathes out short. The work isn't changing the breath. It's knowing it while it happens. Then, step by step, the same breath carries more: calming the body, feeling joy, watching the mind, seeing that all of it changes. In the sutta this one practice, followed far enough, leads all the way to awakening. That's the teaching, named plainly. Buddhists call it anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out, and in the sutta it's both where the path starts and what the elders keep coming back to. So the puzzle solves itself. The breath isn't the beginner's toy you outgrow. It's the one object that is always here, at the root of a tree or at the edge of a bed, so the elders use it too. Sati, the Pali word in its name, means mindfulness: staying with what is happening while it happens. And your phone is very good at pulling you somewhere else. Three breaths, known as breaths, is a small morning version of what the Buddha taught on that full-moon night.
screen: `DON'T CHANGE THE BREATH. KNOW IT.` · `LONG AS LONG, SHORT AS SHORT.` · `THE SAME BREATH LEADS ALL THE WAY.` · `ANAPANASATI: ALWAYS HERE.` · then, large: `BREATH BEFORE PHONE.`

segments.voice: Sit up straight and let the breath come on its own. For each breath, know it the way the sutta says: breathing in long, I know it's long; breathing out short, I know it's short. Don't fix anything, and when your mind drifts to the phone, come back to the very next breath.
A morning breath: the breath you already have, known as it comes and goes, before the day takes you. In the Buddha's teaching, anapanasati.
Your line: breath before phone. Three breaths, known as breaths, and then the screen. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in a number of schools teach anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, asking students to know the breath rather than control it, as the Anapanasati Sutta describes.

Anapanasati Sutta.meaning: the Buddha's discourse on mindfulness of breathing

Savatthi.meaning: a city in ancient India where the Buddha taught

Sariputta.meaning: one of the Buddha's senior disciples

rainy-season retreat.meaning: the monsoon months when Buddhist monks stay in one place
